name: Gastric plication

lead: Gastric plication reduces stomach volume by folding the stomach wall inward and stitching it, rather than cutting out part of it. It is a bariatric (weight-loss) procedure, done laparoscopically or with an endoscope.

Its appearance payoff comes through weight loss: less body fat means a leaner body and often a slimmer face and more visible bone structure. Trials and reviews report weight loss, but a 2018 meta-analysis found sleeve gastrectomy produced greater loss with fewer complications.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon or endoscopist in a clinic or hospital setting as part of a supervised weight-management programme, and is followed by dietary stages and long-term follow-up. Endoscopic variants include techniques such as endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty.

Reported problems include complications, reoperation, inadequate weight loss and, historically, a case report of Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy after plication. Guidelines advise multidisciplinary care with long-term follow-up.

chain: Stomach folded to a smaller volume
Leaner body and face, more visible bone structure
angle.text: Plication is used to lose fat when diet and exercise have not been enough. As body fat falls, features such as the jaw and cheekbones become more visible and the body slimmer.

lead: Gastric plication is a restrictive bariatric procedure in which the stomach is folded inward and sutured to reduce its volume, achieving restriction without stapling, banding or resection [1]. Endoscopic versions use endoluminal sutures and include endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty and the primary obesity surgery endolumenal (POSE) procedure [2].

People interested in appearance come to it for the chain it sets off: smaller stomach, lower food intake, fat loss, then a leaner body and face. Weight loss is the mechanism; the procedure itself does not change facial structure.

It sits among a family of bariatric operations. Wikipedia lists gastric plication with adjustable bands and balloons, while sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass are the most common standard procedures [3].

paras: In a feasibility study of laparoscopic plication, the anterior stomach wall was folded inward from the fundus to the antrum with two rows of sutures in one method, with a second method also tested [4]. A surgeon reporting a 12-year personal experience described modifications such as one-row bilateral plication and the question of including or excluding the right gastroepiploic artery [5].

A report titled Gastric plication for morbid obesity appeared in the Journal of the Kansas Medical Society in 1976 [6]. A 1982 JAMA report described Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy after gastric plication [7]. Laparoscopic versions were studied from around 2010 [4][5]. Endoscopic approaches such as transoral gastric volume reduction were reported in an 18-patient feasibility study [8].

A review of endoscopic plication techniques concluded they are effective for weight loss, with potentially higher efficacy than medications and lifestyle change and lower invasiveness than surgery, and recommended use within a multidisciplinary programme with long-term follow-up [2].

A 2018 meta-analysis of 12 studies compared laparoscopic plication with sleeve gastrectomy and found sleeve gastrectomy had lower overall complications and higher percent excess weight loss, with no difference in hospital stay, operative duration, reoperation or cost; the authors called for larger randomised trials [9]. A systematic review of plication for morbid obesity and a randomised trial against mini-gastric bypass have also been published [10][11].

The meta-analysis above found a higher overall complication rate for plication than for sleeve gastrectomy [9]. A report on short-term outcomes stresses the importance of postoperative follow-up [12]. Nutritional deficiency complications, including the Wernicke-Korsakoff case report, have been documented [7].

The ESSENTIAL trial, a randomised sham-controlled study, evaluated endoscopic plication (the POSE procedure) in people with class I to II obesity, with all subjects receiving low-intensity lifestyle therapy; endpoints were percent total body weight loss at 12 months and the share achieving at least 5% [13]. A 2018 meta-analysis compared laparoscopic plication with sleeve gastrectomy [9], and a randomised trial compared it with mini-gastric bypass [11]. A European guideline's network meta-analysis covered plication among several bariatric options [14]. Registered trials include studies of plication in adolescents, combined with banding, and endoscopic suturing devices [15][16].
